title: National Maritime Union of America v. Commander, Military Sealift Command (1987)
shortTitle: National Maritime Union v. Military Sealift Command
summary: Conflicting interests among an association's members do not by themselves defeat its associational standing, but the members' injury must still be fairly traceable to the challenged illegality and redressable by the relief sought.
notes:
Key line: Judge Bork: "For the reasons given, we think that the mere fact of conflicting interests among members of an association does not of itself defeat the association's standing to urge the interests of some members in litigation, even though success may harm the legal interests of other members."

Citation: 824 F.2d 1228 (D.C. Cir. 1987).

sections.Parties: The appellants were three labor unions: the National Maritime Union of America, AFL-CIO, which represented unlicensed seamen on nine of the twelve ships involved; District No. 1, Pacific Coast District, Marine Engineers' Beneficial Association, which represented licensed engineers; and District No. 3, Radio Officers Union, which represented radio officers. They represented civil service mariners and employees of a losing bidder, Marine Transport Lines, but no employees of the winning bidder. The appellees were the Commander of the Military Sealift Command, a unit of the Navy, the Lavino Shipping Company, which won the contract, and two intervening unions, District 2 of the Marine Engineers' Beneficial Association and the Seafarers International Union, which represented mariners who worked for Lavino or on other ships. Judge Bork wrote for a panel that included Judges Starr and D.H. Ginsburg.
sections.Material Facts: In 1984 the Military Sealift Command operated twelve government owned oceanographic ships with permanent and temporary civil service mariners. Under OMB Circular A-76 it compared the cost of private operation with continued government operation and solicited bids. It tentatively awarded the contract to Marine Transport Lines, and displaced employees and their unions appealed administratively and lost. The Government then concluded that the Service Contract Act applied, rescinded the award, and resolicited with a requirement that the winner pay wages and benefits the Labor Department would later determine, retroactive to the award, because no wage schedule could be prepared in time. On the new offers Lavino was low bidder and won. MSC refused a second administrative appeal because all issues could have been raised in the first, and read the contractual right of first refusal for displaced government employees to cover permanent but not temporary mariners, so that temporary workers would not compete with permanent ones for scarce jobs.
sections.Procedural History: The unions sued in the District Court for the District of Columbia to have the Lavino award declared void and its performance enjoined, seeking resolicitation with a wage determination or, alternatively, an administrative appeal and first refusal rights for temporary mariners. On cross motions for summary judgment the District Court dismissed for lack of standing, holding that the unions were outside the zone of interests of the Service Contract Act because they did not represent the winning bidder's employees, and that Circular A-76 was a managerial tool creating no protected private interest. The D.C. Circuit heard argument on December 11, 1986 and affirmed on July 31, 1987, agreeing that the unions lacked standing on the Service Contract Act claim and rejecting the Circular A-76 claims on the merits without deciding standing.
sections.Issue: The standing questions were layered. First, does an association lose the representational standing recognized in Hunt v. Washington State Apple Advertising Commission when the relief it seeks would help some of its members and hurt others, as the request for first refusal rights for temporary mariners would harm the permanent mariners the same unions represented? Second, is the loss of jobs suffered by the unions' members fairly traceable to the omission of a wage determination from the Lavino contract and redressable by an order setting the award aside, given that the low bidder might win again and the losing bidder was not before the court? Third, could the unions' claims under OMB Circular A-76 survive on the merits.
sections.Holding: The court held that the mere fact of conflicting interests among members does not of itself defeat an association's standing to urge the interests of some members, even though success may harm others, so the unions had associational standing so long as their members would have standing individually. It then held that the members lacked Article III standing on the Service Contract Act claim because their injury, the loss of present or future jobs, was neither fairly traceable to the missing wage determination nor likely to be redressed by resolicitation, which depended on speculative choices by Marine Transport, the Labor Department and the Government. Assuming standing on the Circular A-76 claims, the court held that MSC reasonably denied a futile second appeal and reasonably read the first refusal provision to reach permanent but not temporary employees.
sections.Reasoning: Judge Bork reasoned that the Supreme Court had probably settled the conflict question in UAW v. Brock, where it acknowledged that an association's litigating position might reflect only a majority or an influential minority yet preserved associational standing because its benefits were too valuable to jettison, suggesting safeguards for dissenting members instead. Independently, most associations have internal conflicts that they resolve through their own procedures, and members accept the resulting harms as the cost of association; courts uphold such internal resolutions unless the organization's procedures were violated, and litigating positions are no different. Dissenting members could intervene, challenge the association's compliance with its own procedures, or in the union setting invoke the duty of fair representation, though that duty reaches only matters within the union's exclusive bargaining authority and was not implicated here. On causation, the Service Contract Act protects only the winning bidder's employees, whom the unions did not represent, and the unions' real injury was job loss from the award itself. Nothing suggested Lavino would have lost had a wage determination been included, Marine Transport had not joined the suit and might not rebid, the Government's cost estimate was unaffected by the Act, and the effect of a future wage determination on the bids was unknowable. These independent variables made the injury speculative under Warth v. Seldin and Mideast Systems.

topics.lrs-n-standing-association: Member conflict calls for attention to representation and process but does not itself eliminate standing.

learning.why: The course reads it for the associational standing rule that internal disagreement among members does not bar an organization from suing, and as an illustration of how traceability and redressability can fail when the outcome depends on third parties not before the court.
